doc.title: James Moody — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Painted faces and "war paint" on the bandstand
summary: Moody criticizes groups who paint their faces, saying it has nothing to do with music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Is jazz healthy? Young players, rock and the future

blocks.x: That stuff, man, that stuff is out! Because too many, like, first of all your -- your husband, David, knew people that go over teaching music, people don't come over with that crap. You play some music for me.
You're talking about groups like the Art Ensemble and?
Well, I don't know what -- what the groups are, but they -­
I don't know who they are. I just see people with painted faces, they're playing. What has that got to do with music?

Especially a saxophone. Like, if you're going to play the woodwind and you're going to chew the bow and arrow or something, then you know, but I mean, if you're gonna play jazz, still has nothing to do with the [indiscernible], when your face is painted, I mean, as far as I think or know, that's like when you're going to war. When I get ready to play music, I'm going to -- to do something, like, you know, pleasant and loving, hopefully. You know, rather than, you know, like, because that's what paint is. War paint. People don't paint their faces like that to go and -- and be friendly. I mean, that's, you know. I mean, maybe some African women might put a little paint here or something just a little thing, but not -- when you paint your face like that, everywhere, that's so you can look fierce in battle. You know.
